# Axis keys


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

An array can have string keys on any of its axes. A key names one
position on its axis. The position still has its number, counting from
0. Functions keep their ordinary meanings, and their results keep the
keys.

## Construction

[`:`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/colon.html) puts the
keys on its left onto the leading axis of the array on its right.
Several keys name the major cells. This table is a vector of two
columns, each keyed by its name:

``` bpl
T←"price" "qty":[[1 2 3] [4 5 6]]
T
≢T
```

    ["price":[1 2 3] "qty":[4 5 6]]

    2ₓ

With a single key,
[`:`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/colon.html) makes the
whole right argument the one item of a keyed vector:

``` bpl
"ab":11 12 13
ρ"ab":11 12 13
```

    ["ab":[11 12 13]]

    [1]ₓ

On a matrix, the keys name the rows:

``` bpl
"price" "qty":2 3ρι6ₓ
```

        ₓ      
    price 0 1 2
      qty 3 4 5

You can write a keyed vector the way it is displayed, as a bracket list
of `key:value` items. In `["aa":1 2]`, the `2` has no key. The empty
record is `⍬:⍬`.

``` bpl
T≡["price":1 2 3;"qty":4 5 6]
["kind":"bar"]≡"kind":"bar"
```

    $t

    $t

A record inside a vector needs its own brackets, as in `[15 ["aa":1]]`.

A character or a string is one key. `'a' 'b'` is the single key `"ab"`,
because characters side by side form one string. Write `"a" "b"` for two
keys. A numeric subscript chooses an axis. `ι₀` lists the keys of axis
0:

``` bpl
ι₀'a' 'b':1 2
ι₀"a" "b":1 2
```

    ["ab"]

    "a" "b"

`K:⍠axis A` puts keys on any axis of `A`. Here they name the columns:

``` bpl
m←"Jan" "Feb" "Mar":⍠1⁝2 3ρι6ₓ
m
```

    ₓ Jan Feb Mar
        0   1   2
        3   4   5

Selecting [`:`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/colon.html)
on the first axis and `"Feb"` on the second gives the Feb column:

``` bpl
[: "Feb"]⌷m
```

    [1 4]ₓ

Several key vectors label successive axes. Write them inside one pair of
brackets, with `;` between them, because each one contains spaces:

``` bpl
M←["alice" "bob";"price" "qty"]:[10 2◇20 4]
M
```

          price qty
    alice    10   2
      bob    20   4

`ι₀ ₁` lists the keys of both axes:

``` bpl
ι₀ ₁M
```

    ("alice" "bob"◇"price" "qty")

[`:`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/colon.html) takes
several axes in the order given. This builds the same `M` by giving the
column keys before the row keys:

``` bpl
M≡["price" "qty";"alice" "bob"]:₁ ₀[10 2◇20 4]
```

    $t

[`:`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/colon.html) removes
every key and axis name:

``` bpl
:M
```

    10 2
    20 4

`:₁` removes only axis 1’s keys and name:

``` bpl
:₁M
```

    alice 10 2
      bob 20 4

For an axis without keys,
[`ι`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/iota.html) lists its
positions:

``` bpl
ι₀ ₁:M
```

    (0 1◇0 1)ₓ

A dfn can build a record with
[`:`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/colon.html) like any
other code:

``` bpl
{"total":+/ω}1 2 3
{+/:ω}"aa" "bb":1 2
```

    ["total":6]

    3

Keys on one axis must be unique strings, one for each position:

<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Expression</th>
<th>Error</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>"aa" "aa":1 2</code></td>
<td><code>DOMAIN</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>"aa" "bb":₀[1 2 3]</code></td>
<td><code>LENGTH</code></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Selection and assignment

Index [`⌷`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/squad.html)
takes a key or a position for each leading axis. Selecting a single key
or position removes its axis. The key `"bob"` and the position `1`
select the same row:

``` bpl
"bob"⌷M
1⌷M
```

    ["price":20 "qty":4]

    ["price":20 "qty":4]

Selecting on both axes gives one item.
[`:`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/colon.html) selects a
whole axis. Keys and positions can be mixed:

``` bpl
"alice" "qty"⌷M
[: "qty"]⌷M
"bob" 0⌷M
```

    2

    ["alice":2 "bob":4]

    20

Selecting with a vector keeps the axis. A string counts as one key.
Selecting the same item more than once, by key or by position, drops the
selected axis’s keys, as [Index](glyphs/squad.qmd) describes. To select
one row and keep the axis, use a one-item vector of keys:

``` bpl
[,⊂"alice"]⌷M
```

          price qty
    alice    10   2

Pick [`⊃`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/right-shoe.html)
selects by key too. One key picks a row as a record:

``` bpl
"bob" "qty"⊃M
"bob"⊃M
```

    4

    ["price":20 "qty":4]

Dot indexing puts the selection after the array, with one bracket item
for each axis. `M.["alice" "qty"]` is `"alice" "qty"⌷M`. A path of names
after a dot, as in `rec.addr.city`, picks by each name in turn through
nested records:

``` bpl
rec←["n":1 "addr":["city":"LA"]]
rec.addr.city
M.["alice" "qty"]
```

    "LA"

    2

After a function, `.name` reads a field of the function’s result. Paths
work as they do after an array. `⊢.addr.city` means `{ω.addr.city}`:

``` bpl
⊢.addr.city rec
```

    "LA"

This lets you read a field inside an operator without writing a dfn. Any
function can come before the
[`.`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/dot.html):

``` bpl
orders←[["price":10 "qty":2] ["price":5 "qty":1]]
⊢.price¨ orders
•json.price "{""price"":10.5}"
```

    10 5

    10.5

When the name after the
[`.`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/dot.html) holds a
function, the expression is an inner product instead, as `+.×` is.
[Indexing](indexing.ipynb) shows `f.[I]`, which selects from a
function’s result.

Modified assignment works through a dot path:

``` bpl
rec.n+←1
rec.n
```

    2

Plain assignment through a dot path creates any missing keys and records
along the path:

``` bpl
rec.style.color←"red"
rec.style
```

    ["color":"red"]

On an axis without keys, the new position gets a key and the existing
positions have none:

``` bpl
v←10 20 30
v.x←9
v
```

    [10 20 30 "x":9]

Plain assignment through dot indexing appends a missing row or column,
as assignment through
[`⌷`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/squad.html) does. New
cells start as the array’s [prototype](terms.qmd#term-prototype) until
the assignment fills them. Here the first assignment adds a row for
cara, and the second a tax column:

``` bpl
N←M
N.["cara"]←30 5
N.[: "tax"]←1 2 3
N
```

          price qty tax
    alice    10   2   1
      bob    20   4   2
     cara    30   5   3

Assigning to a new row and a new column at once adds both. The assigned
cell gets the value, and the other new cells hold the prototype:

``` bpl
P←M
P.["cara" "tax"]←3
P
```

          price qty tax
    alice    10   2   0
      bob    20   4   0
     cara     0   0   3

Reading a missing key gives the fill. Modified assignment at a missing
key adds the key, starting from the fill, as `x←x f y` would. Assignment
to a position past the end changes nothing, because a position can’t
extend an axis. For `T←"aa" "bb":1 2`:

<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Expression</th>
<th>Result</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>"cc"⌷T</code></td>
<td><code>0</code>, the fill</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>T.["cc"]+←1</code></td>
<td>adds <code>"cc"</code> holding <code>1</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>T.[2]←9</code></td>
<td><code>T</code> unchanged</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

Assigning to a single key or position stores the whole right argument
there. Assigning to a vector selection aligns the kept axis with the
right argument’s keys. The same keyed `u` gives a different result each
way:

``` bpl
u←"bb" "aa":8 9
t←"aa" "bb":1 2
t.["aa"]←u
"aa"⌷t
```

    ["bb":8 "aa":9]

``` bpl
tt←"aa" "bb":1 2
tt.[,⊂"aa"]←u
"aa"⌷tt
```

    9

## Agreement

When both arguments of a pervasive function have keys on an axis, they
align by key. The result lists the left argument’s keys, then the keys
only the right argument has. A missing entry is read as the prototype of
the array it is missing from:

``` bpl
["aa":2] + ["bb":3]
["aa":2] × ["bb":3]
["aa":0] = ["bb":0]
```

    ["aa":2 "bb":3]

    ["aa":0 "bb":0]

    ["aa":$t "bb":$t]

[`⍠`](glyphs/quad-colon.qmd#fill) with an options record chooses the
fill for one call. The fill takes the type of the argument that reads
it:

``` bpl
["aa":2] +⍠["fill":10] ["bb":3]
["aa":2] ×⍠["fill":1] ["bb":3]
```

    ["aa":12 "bb":13]

    ["aa":2 "bb":3]

Keys in a different order still line up:

``` bpl
["aa":1 "bb":2] + ["bb":10 "aa":20]
```

    ["aa":21 "bb":12]

Each keyed axis aligns on its own. Two one-cell matrices with no keys in
common add up to a 2×2 matrix:

``` bpl
a←[["alice"] ["price"]]:1 1ρ10
b←[["bob"] ["qty"]]:1 1ρ2
a+b
```

          price qty
    alice    10   0
      bob     0   2

When one argument has no keys on an axis, agreement goes by position. A
keyed singleton is stretched to match the other argument and loses its
key. Enclosing the other argument keeps the key and puts the sum inside
it:

``` bpl
["base":5] + 10 20 30
["base":5] + ⊂10 20 30
["aa":1 "bb":2] + 10 20
```

    15 25 35

    ["base":[15 25 35]]

    ["aa":11 "bb":22]

An axis operand chooses which axes correspond. Lined up with the columns
of `M`, the keyed vector is added to the qty column, and the result has
a new tax column:

``` bpl
M+₁"qty" "tax":10 2
```

          price qty tax
    alice    10  12   2
      bob    20  14   2

## Array operations

Transpose moves each axis with its keys:

``` bpl
Mᵀ
```

          alice bob
    price    10  20
      qty     2   4

Reverse, rotate, take, drop and filtering move keys with their
positions:

``` bpl
scores←"aa" "bb" "cc":10 20 5
⌽scores
1⌽scores
¯1↑scores
1↓scores
1 0 1#scores
```

    ["cc":5 "bb":20 "aa":10]

    ["bb":20 "cc":5 "aa":10]

    ["cc":5]

    ["bb":20 "cc":5]

    ["aa":10 "cc":5]

Reduction removes the reduced axis and its keys:

``` bpl
+/M
+⌿M
```

    ["alice":12 "bob":24]

    ["price":30 "qty":6]

Scan and Each keep their argument’s keys:

``` bpl
+\scores
+/¨["price":1 2 3;"qty":4 5 6]
```

    ["aa":10 "bb":30 "cc":35]

    ["price":6 "qty":15]

Reshape keeps the keys only when the shape is unchanged. Ravel drops the
keys of the axes it merges. Table keeps the keys of the axis it leaves
alone:

``` bpl
pair←"aa" "bb":1 2
2ρpair
4ρpair
,"aa" "bb":2 2ρι4ₓ
ι₀⍪"aa" "bb":2 2ρι4ₓ
```

    ["aa":1 "bb":2]

    1 2 1 2

    [0 1 2 3]ₓ

    "aa" "bb"

Rank keeps the keys of the frame. An axis inside the result cells keeps
a key only when every cell has that key in the same place. Pairing each
item of `pair` with itself keeps the row keys:

``` bpl
,⍨⁰ pair
```

    aa 1 1
    bb 2 2

Reversing each row of `M` moves the column keys to the same positions in
every row, so the result keeps them:

``` bpl
⌽¹ M
```

          qty price
    alice   2    10
      bob   4    20

Reversing only alice’s row loses the column keys, because the two rows
now have them in different orders:

``` bpl
{10=↑ω?⌽ω;ω}¹ M
```

    alice  2 10
      bob 20  4

A rotation with a different count for each row drops the rotated axis’s
keys in the same way:

``` bpl
0 1⌽M
```

    alice 10  2
      bob  4 20

Outer product keeps both arguments’ axes and their keys:

``` bpl
["aa":1 "bb":2] +⊗ ["xx":10 "yy":20]
```

       xx yy
    aa 11 21
    bb 12 22

An array of Power counts supplies the result’s frame, with its keys:

``` bpl
counts←"initial" "once" "twice":0 1 2
⊽⍣counts 3
```

    ["initial":3 "once":6 "twice":12]

Inner product, Decode and matrix solve align the keys of the axes they
contract. When both arguments have keys on the contracted axes, the key
sets must be equal, or the call raises a `LENGTH` error. When either
argument has none, the contraction goes by position:

``` bpl
["hi":1 "lo":2] +.× ["lo":10 "hi":20]
["hi":10 "lo":10] ⊥ ["lo":2 "hi":1]
```

    40

    12

Solving against `S`, which has keys on both axes, gives a vector keyed
by `S`’s column keys:

``` bpl
S←["r1" "r2";"xx" "yy"]:[2 0◇0 4]ₓ
["r2":12 "r1":4]ₓ ⌹ S
```

    ["xx":2 "yy":3]

Inverting `S` swaps its row and column keys:

``` bpl
⌹S
```

        r1   r2
    xx 0.5    0
    yy   0 0.25

Catenate joins the keys along its axis and aligns the other keyed axes.
A position from an unkeyed part has no key:

``` bpl
["aa":1] , ["bb":2]
["aa":1 "bb":2] , 5
```

    ["aa":1 "bb":2]

    ["aa":1 "bb":2 5]

`B` lists its rows in the opposite order from `A`:

``` bpl
A←["aa" "bb";"xx" "yy"]:[1 2◇3 4]
B←["bb" "aa";["zz"]]:[[5]◇[6]]
A,B
```

       xx yy zz
    aa  1  2  6
    bb  3  4  5

Replicate can repeat the items of an unkeyed axis, and the other axes
keep their keys:

``` bpl
2#₋₁["aa" "bb"]:[1 2◇3 4]
```

    aa 1 1 2 2
    bb 3 3 4 4

Positions added by Take, [expand](glyphs/hash.qmd#expand) or fill from
an unkeyed part have no keys:

``` bpl
3↑pair
1 0 1#⁻pair
```

    ["aa":1 "bb":2 0]

    ["aa":1 0 "bb":2]

Catenate and Replicate cannot construct an axis with repeated keys. For
`V←"aa" "bb":1 2`:

<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Expression</th>
<th>Reason</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>V,V</code></td>
<td>Duplicate joined keys</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>2#V</code></td>
<td>Repeated keys</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

### Windows

Full windows add an unkeyed axis of window positions. The axis that a
window slides along loses its keys in every window:

``` bpl
w←"aa" "bb" "cc":1 2 3
2↕w
```

    1 2
    2 3

Even a single window of 3, which covers every key, loses those keys:

``` bpl
3↕w
```

    1 2 3

Each padded window is keyed by its centre:

``` bpl
¯3↕w
```

    aa 0 1 2
    bb 1 2 3
    cc 2 3 0

Each item of a stencil’s result has the key of the position at the
centre of its window. Inside the operand, a window has no keys along the
axes it slides on:

``` bpl
+/⌺3 w
{ι₀ω ≡ ι3ₓ}⌺3 w
```

    ["aa":3 "bb":6 "cc":5]

    ["aa":$t "bb":$t "cc":$t]

## Match and search

Before comparing, Match aligns keys on every axis where both arguments
have keys. An axis without keys matches a keyed axis by position. Axis
names match by the same rule used to pair axes in arithmetic: two axes
match when they have the same name or either has none. A keyed vector
matches its reverse, because its keys move with its values, and it
matches the same values without keys:

``` bpl
levels←"low" "mid" "high":10 20 30
levels≡⌽levels
levels≡10 20 30
```

    $t

    $t

Searches compare values or cells and return the key of a position where
a match is found. For a value that isn’t found, the search returns the
length, as usual:

``` bpl
levelsι20 99
levels⍸5 15 25 40
```

    "mid" 3ₓ

    0ₓ "low" "mid" "high"

Grade down lists the keys from the largest value to the smallest:

``` bpl
⍒levels
[⍒levels]⌷levels
```

    "high" "mid" "low"

    ["high":30 "mid":20 "low":10]

Membership compares values and keeps the left argument’s keys:

``` bpl
["aa":7] ∊ ["bb":7]
```

    ["aa":$t]

A position in a matrix can contain both keys and numbers. Iota without a
subscript still takes its argument’s values as a shape, whatever keys
the argument has:

``` bpl
Q←"price" "qty":₁[10 2◇20 4]
↑⍸Q=20
ι"rows" "cols":2 3
```

    1ₓ "price"

    [0 0] [0 1] [0 2]
    [1 0] [1 1] [1 2]

Unique and the set functions compare values and keep the keys of the
positions they select:

``` bpl
p←"aa" "bb":1 2
q←"xx" "yy":2 3
p∩q
p~q
p∪q
∪"aa" "bb" "cc":1 1 2
```

    ["bb":2]

    ["aa":1]

    ["aa":1 "bb":2 "yy":3]

    ["aa":1 "cc":2]

Monadic Key passes the keys of each group’s positions to its operand.
Dyadic Key keeps the keys on the grouped values:

``` bpl
k←"aa" "bb" "cc":1 2 1
{⊂ω}⌸k
1 2 1{⊂ω}⌸k
```

    ("aa" "cc"◇"bb")

    ("aa":1 "cc":1◇"bb":2)

## Named axes

An axis name identifies a dimension, such as `city`, while its keys
identify positions along it, such as `LA` and `NY`. Axis names are
unique within an array.

An array’s shape is keyed by its axis names. Reshaping by a keyed shape
names the axes:

``` bpl
C←["city":2 "month":3]ρι6ₓ
ρC
"month"⌷ρC
```

    ["city":2 "month":3]ₓ

    3ₓ

An axis operand can name an axis instead of numbering it:

``` bpl
+/⍠"month" C
```

    ["city":2]ρ[3 12]ₓ

An entry of the shape without a key leaves its axis unnamed. `N:ρA ρ A`
renames the axes. `:ρA ρ A` removes only the names, and `ρA ρ :A` only
the position keys. A whole-number key equal to its position stands for
no key, as the `1` in `"city" 1` does. A reshape that keeps the shape
also keeps the position keys and shares the array’s storage:

``` bpl
ρ "city" 1:ρC ρ C
ρ :ρC ρ C
```

    ["city":2 3]ₓ

    [2 3]ₓ

A keyed vector to the left of
[`:`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/colon.html) uses each
key as an axis name and that key’s value as the axis’s position keys:

``` bpl
sales←["city":"NY" "LA";"month":"Jan" "Feb" "Mar"]:[10 20 30◇40 50 60]
sales
```

       Jan Feb Mar
    NY  10  20  30
    LA  40  50  60

The shape of `sales` is keyed by axis name, and its positions are
identified by keys:

``` bpl
ρsales
"LA" "Feb"⌷sales
```

    ["city":2 "month":3]ₓ

    50

An axis description can be kept in a name and reused, or attached to
chosen axes. The other axes keep their names and keys:

``` bpl
months←"month":"Jan" "Feb" "Mar"
D←months:₁2 3ρι6ₓ
ρD
ρ("city":"NY" "LA"):D
```

    [2 "month":3]ₓ

    ["city":2 "month":3]ₓ

A record of several axes attaches to the chosen axes in the order given:

``` bpl
axes←["month":"Jan" "Feb" "Mar";"city":"NY" "LA"]
ρaxes:₁ ₀ 2 3ρι6ₓ
```

    ["city":2 "month":3]ₓ

Agreement first pairs axes with equal names, wherever they sit. Unpaired
axes broadcast. When every axis of the left argument pairs and the right
argument has more axes, the result has the right argument’s axis order.
Otherwise the left argument’s axes come first, then the axes only the
right argument has:

``` bpl
monthly←["month":3]ρ10 20 30
C+monthly
```

    10 21 32
    13 24 35

`monthly+C` has the order of `C`, the larger argument, as `C+monthly`
does. When the arguments have the same axes, the result has the left
argument’s order, and `C+Cᵀ` pairs each axis with the one of the same
name:

``` bpl
ρmonthly+C
C+Cᵀ
```

    ["city":2 "month":3]ₓ

    [0 2  4
     6 8 10]ₓ

The remaining axes pair in leading-axis order. A named axis paired with
an unnamed one keeps its name. Length agreement and key alignment then
apply as usual:

``` bpl
C+10 20
```

    10 11 12
    23 24 25

Axes with different names stay separate, each broadcasting against the
other:

``` bpl
ρ ["city":2 3]ρ1 + ["product":4 3]ρ2
```

    ["city":2 3 "product":4]ₓ

Use a name or a list of names as the
[`⍠`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/quad-colon.html)
operand to specify axes. Index with that operand selects positions on
the named axes:

``` bpl
L←["city":"LA" "NY";"month":"Jan" "Feb" "Mar"]:2 3ρι6ₓ
"LA"⌷⍠"city" L
"LA"⌷L ≡ "LA"⌷⍠"city" L
ρ⊂⍠"month" L
+/⍠"city" "month" L
```

    ["month":3]ρ["Jan":0 "Feb":1 "Mar":2]ₓ

    $t

    ["city":2]ₓ

    15ₓ

Transpose moves names with their axes. Selecting with a single key or
position removes the axis and its name. Replicate and Table keep the
name. Reshape takes the axis names from its left argument. Ravel drops
the names of the axes it merges. New axes start unnamed:

``` bpl
ρCᵀ
ρ0⌷C
ρ2 3ρC
ρ,C
cities←["city":2]ρ1 2
ρ2#cities
ρ⍪cities
```

    ["month":3 "city":2]ₓ

    ["month":3]ₓ

    [2 3]ₓ

    [6]ₓ

    ["city":4]ₓ

    ["city":2 1]ₓ

When an operation gives two axes the same name, both lose it. Their
position keys remain:

``` bpl
lanes←["city":2]ρ"LA" "NY":1 2
ρlanes×⊗lanes
ι₀ ₁lanes×⊗lanes
```

    [2 2]ₓ

    ("LA" "NY"◇"LA" "NY")

Applying [`ι`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/iota.html)
to a keyed shape gives a named index: the positions of an axis, arranged
along an axis of that name. Named indices let a formula read as it does
in index notation. A named index used alone in a selection reads the
axis with that name, wherever it stands in the brackets. The result’s
axis keeps that name. Selectors that share a name pair with each other
and read the data’s axes in order, as `m.[i i]` below does. Reading at a
position outside its axis returns the fill, as for any selector. As the
[`⍠`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/quad-colon.html)
operand, a named index specifies its axis:

``` bpl
i←ι["i":3] ◇ j←ι["j":3]
ρi+10×j
m←[0 1 2◇3 4 5◇6 7 8]
m.[i i]
+/⍠i m.[i i]
x←10ₓ×ι5ₓ ◇ k←ι["k":4]
x.[k+1ₓ]-x.[k]
month←ι⍠"month" sales ◇ city←ι⍠"city" sales
sales≡sales.[month city]
```

    ["i":3 "j":3]ₓ

    ["i":3]ρ[0 4 8]

    12

    ["k":4]ρ[10 10 10 10]ₓ

    $t

[`•index`](system/index.qmd) gives an index with a new axis name that
starts with `_` and cannot collide with names on the caller’s data.
Plain display leaves that name out. Box mode and
[`ρ`](https://answerdotai.github.io/basedpl/glyphs/rho.html) show it
shortened, as in `_·…`. Indices with different names build a grid, here
of the differences between every pair of items:

``` bpl
y←10 20 40 ◇ [r c]←•index 3 3
y.[r]-y.[c]
```

     0 ¯10 ¯30
    10   0 ¯20
    30  20   0

## Python and JSON

`Array` converts Python dicts to keyed vectors recursively. `.py`
converts them back to dicts.

``` python
from basedpl import Array
import numpy as np

record = Array({'price': 10, 'address': {'city': 'LA'}})
assert record.py == {'price': 10, 'address': {'city': 'LA'}}
assert record.keys == (('price', 'address'),)
```

Pass `keys` to `Array` to attach position keys, and `names` to attach
axis names. `None` leaves an axis without keys or a name. The `.keys`
and `.names` properties return the position keys and axis names. `.np`
copies the values to NumPy.

``` python
rows, cols = ['NY', 'LA'], ['Jan', 'Feb', 'Mar']
data = [[10, 20, 30], [40, 50, 60]]
sales = Array(data, keys=(rows, cols), names=('city', 'month'))
assert sales.keys == (tuple(rows), tuple(cols))
assert sales.names == ('city', 'month')
assert sales.np.tolist() == data
columns_only = Array(data, keys=(None, cols), names=(None, 'month'))
assert columns_only.keys == (None, tuple(cols))
assert columns_only.names == (None, 'month')
```

`.df` converts to a pandas DataFrame. For a matrix, the position keys
become the row and column labels, and the axis names become the names of
the index and the columns. `.py` uses this conversion for keyed arrays
of rank 2 or more. Install pandas with `pip install pandas`. basedpl
imports pandas only when converting.

``` python
df = sales.df
assert df.loc['LA', 'Feb'] == 50
assert (df.index.name, df.columns.name) == ('city', 'month')
assert sales.py.equals(df)
assert columns_only.df.index.tolist() == [0, 1]
```

Above rank 2, the last axis supplies the columns, and the earlier axes
form a row MultiIndex. Unkeyed axes use labels that count from 0. Units
and vectors become one-column DataFrames.

``` python
counts = np.arange(12).reshape(2, 2, 3)
names = 'year', 'city', 'month'
cube = Array(counts, keys=(None, rows, cols), names=names)
assert cube.df.index.names == ['year', 'city']
assert cube.df.loc[(1, 'LA'), 'Mar'] == 11
assert Array({'aa': 1, 'bb': 2}).df.loc['bb', 0] == 2
assert Array(7).df.loc[0, 0] == 7
```

[`•json`](data.ipynb#json) converts ordinary JSON objects to keyed
vectors. The [process protocol](processes.qmd) includes `axis_keys` and
`axis_names` alongside the shape, row-major data and prototype. For
`sales` above:

``` json
{
  "shape": [2, 3],
  "data": [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60],
  "prototype": 0,
  "axis_keys": [["NY", "LA"], ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar"]],
  "axis_names": ["city", "month"]
}
```

Use `null` for an axis without keys or a name. Omit `axis_keys` when no
axis has keys, and `axis_names` when no axis has a name:

``` json
{"shape":[1,2],"data":[10,20],"prototype":0,"axis_keys":[null,["Jan","Feb"]]}
{"shape":[2],"data":[10,20],"prototype":0}
```
